```{r setup, include=T, message = F, warning = F, echo = F}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = knitr::is_html_output(),
  fig.align = "center",
  fig.path = "../Figures/report/",

theme_matt = function(base_size = 18,
                      dark_text = "grey20"){
  mid_text <-  monochromeR::generate_palette(dark_text, "go_lighter", n_colours = 5)[2]
  light_text <-  monochromeR::generate_palette(dark_text, "go_lighter", n_colours = 5)[3]
  
  ggpubr::theme_pubr(base_family="sans") %+replace% 
    theme(
      panel.background  = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA), 
      plot.background = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA), 
      legend.background = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA),
      legend.key = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA),
      text = element_text(colour = mid_text, lineheight = 1.1),
      title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.5,
                           colour = dark_text),
      axis.text = element_text(size = base_size,
                               colour = mid_text),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = base_size * 1.2,
                                  margin = unit(c(3, 0, 0, 0), "mm")),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = base_size * 1.2,
                                  margin = unit(c(0, 5, 0, 0), "mm"), 
                                  angle = 90),
      legend.text = element_text(size=base_size * 0.9),
      legend.title = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, 
                                  face = "bold"),
      plot.margin = margin(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25,"cm")
    )
}

theme_matt_facets = function(base_size = 18,
                             dark_text = "grey20"){
  mid_text <-  monochromeR::generate_palette(dark_text, "go_lighter", n_colours = 5)[2]
  light_text <-  monochromeR::generate_palette(dark_text, "go_lighter", n_colours = 5)[3]
  
  theme_bw(base_family="sans") %+replace% 
    theme(
      panel.grid = element_blank(),
      panel.background  = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA), 
      plot.background = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA), 
      legend.background = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA),
      legend.key = element_rect(fill="transparent", colour=NA),
      text = element_text(colour = mid_text, lineheight = 1.1),
      strip.text.x = element_text(size = base_size),
      title = element_text(size = base_size * 1.5,
                           colour = dark_text),
      axis.text = element_text(size = base_size,
                               colour = mid_text),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = base_size * 1.2,
                                  margin = unit(c(3, 0, 0, 0), "mm")),
      axis.title.y = element_text(size = base_size * 1.2,
                                  margin = unit(c(0, 5, 0, 0), "mm"), 
                                  angle = 90),
      legend.text = element_text(size=base_size * 0.9),
      legend.title = element_text(size = base_size * 0.9, 
                                  face = "bold"),
      plot.margin = margin(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25,"cm")
    )
}
```

## CTmax Data

```{r}
ctmax_model_data = ctmax_data %>% 
  mutate(treatment = case_when(
    dose_group == "Control" ~ "Control",
    dose_group == "Salt" ~ salt
  ))

ggplot(ctmax_model_data, aes(x = treatment, y = ctmax)) + 
  facet_wrap(species~.) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  geom_point(size = 1) + 
  theme_matt_facets()

```

Shown below are the sample sizes for the various salt-treatment combinations. Fewer experiments were run with Instant Ocean, so the sample sizes are smaller for this salt.

```{r}

ctmax_data %>% 
  count(species, salt, dose_group) %>% 
  knitr::kable()

```

A linear mixed effects model was used to examine variation in CTmax as a function of salt type (Instant Ocean and road salt) and treatment (control or salt-acclimated). We also examined the interaction between these factors to determine whether the effect of treatment depended on the type of salt used. Experiment date was included as a random effect to control for any differences between collections or experimental replicates.

```{r}

salt.model = lmer(data = ctmax_model_data,
                  ctmax ~ species * treatment + (1|assay_date))

knitr::kable(car::Anova(salt.model, type = "III"))

```

The mixed effects model indicates that there was a significant interaction between salt type and treatment. We examined this interaction by calculating the marginal treatment means by salt type. Shown below, there was no significant difference between treatment groups in the Instant Ocean experiments, but there was a substantial difference between treatment groups in the road salt experiments.

```{r}
salt.means = emmeans::emmeans(salt.model, ~ treatment | species) %>% emmeans::contrast(method = "trt.vs.ctrl")

knitr::kable(salt.means)
```

```{r}

salt.means %>%  data.frame() %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = contrast, x = estimate, colour = species)) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = estimate - SE, xmax = estimate + SE),
                width = 0.2, linewidth = 1, 
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) + 
  geom_point(size = 3, 
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) + 
  theme_matt() + 
  theme(legend.position = "right")

```

### Survival 


### Weibull (accelerated failure time) survival model

A Weibull AFT model (`survival::survreg()`) was used to examine how salt type, chloride dose, and species jointly affect survival time.

`L. minutus` was never tested with RoadSalt, so `species:salt` isn't a full 3x3 grid -- one cell has zero observations. Fitting `species * salt * est_chloride` directly leaves that cell's interaction terms unidentifiable (`NA` coefficients), and `predict.survreg()` propagates those `NA`s to *every* row's prediction (`0 * NA = NA` in R, unlike `predict.lm()`, which degrades gracefully). Collapsing `species:salt` into a single factor with `drop = TRUE` removes the empty cell before fitting, so every remaining combination gets its own identifiable intercept and dose slope.

```{r weibull-prep}
surv_model_data = surv_data %>% 
  filter(hour > 0) %>%  # Weibull AFT models time on the log scale; hour == 0 is undefined
  mutate(
    species = factor(species),
    salt = factor(salt),
    exp_date = factor(exp_date),          # for clustering, not as a fixed effect -- too many levels
    group = interaction(species, salt, drop = TRUE)
  )
```

Before trusting the parametric fit, we check the Weibull constant-shape assumption: a roughly straight, parallel set of lines on a complementary log-log scale supports the Weibull model.

```{r weibull-km-check, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
km_fit = survfit(Surv(hour, ind_surv) ~ species + salt, data = surv_model_data)

ggsurvplot(km_fit, data = surv_model_data, fun = "cloglog", facet.by = "salt")
```

```{r weibull-fit}
weibull_fit = survreg(
  Surv(hour, ind_surv) ~ group * est_chloride,
  data = surv_model_data,
  dist = "weibull",
  cluster = exp_date
)

stopifnot("Aliased (NA) coefficients -- check for empty species x salt cells" =
            !anyNA(coef(weibull_fit)))

summary(weibull_fit)
```

`survreg()` coefficients are on the log(time) scale; exponentiating gives the multiplicative change in expected survival time (acceleration factor) -- values below 1 indicate shorter survival time.

```{r}
knitr::kable(exp(coef(weibull_fit)), col.names = "Acceleration factor", digits = 3)
```

### Predicted survivorship across the salinity gradient

Model-predicted survival curves (lines, by day) are overlaid on the observed daily proportional survival (points). Predictions are restricted per species x salt group to hours actually observed in that group, so lines don't extrapolate past the last check.

```{r weibull-pred-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
plot_days = daily_prop_data %>% 
  filter(day > 0) %>% 
  distinct(day) %>% 
  arrange(day) %>% 
  pull(day)

obs_hour_range = daily_prop_data %>% 
  group_by(species, salt) %>% 
  summarise(max_hour = max(hour), .groups = "drop")

group_map = surv_model_data %>% distinct(species, salt, group)

shape = 1 / weibull_fit$scale

pred_grid = obs_hour_range %>% 
  left_join(group_map, by = c("species", "salt")) %>% 
  tidyr::crossing(
    est_chloride = seq(0, max(surv_model_data$est_chloride, na.rm = TRUE), length.out = 100),
    day = plot_days
  ) %>% 
  mutate(hour = day * 24) %>% 
  filter(hour <= max_hour, hour > 0) %>% 
  select(-max_hour)

pred_grid = pred_grid %>% 
  mutate(
    lp = predict(weibull_fit, newdata = pred_grid, type = "lp"),
    surv_prob = 1 - pweibull(hour, shape = shape, scale = exp(lp))
  )

ggplot(pred_grid, aes(x = est_chloride, y = surv_prob, colour = factor(day))) + 
  facet_grid(salt ~ species, scales = "free_x") + 
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "grey") + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) + 
  geom_point(
    data = daily_prop_data %>% filter(day %in% plot_days, day > 0, day < 6),
    aes(x = est_chloride, y = prop_surv, colour = factor(day)),
    alpha = 0.3
  ) + 
  labs(x = "Chloride-equivalent dose (mg/L)", y = "Survival probability", colour = "Day") + 
  theme_matt_facets()
```

Note: the model assumes a single shared Weibull shape parameter across all species/salt/dose combinations (no `strata()` term). If the cloglog diagnostic above shows clearly non-parallel lines across groups, consider refitting with `strata(salt)` (or `strata(group)`) so each group gets its own shape, and update the `shape` term above accordingly.

### LC50 Values 

```{r}

salt_cols = c("MgCl2" = "#761968", 
              "NaCl" = "#32ad3a", 
              "RoadSalt" = "red")

daily_prop_data %>% 
    filter(exp_day != 0) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = est_chloride, y = prop_surv, colour = species, weight = initial)) + 
  facet_grid(exp_day~salt, scales = "free") + 
  geom_point(aes(size = initial), alpha = 0.6)+ 
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",
              method.args = list(family = "quasibinomial"), 
              se = F, 
              linewidth = 2.5)

```

We previously fit a separate logistic regression for each species x salt x day subset and extracted the LC50 (chloride concentration producing 50% mortality) from each with `dose.p()`. That approach has two problems: (1) each `glm(prop_surv ~ est_chloride, family = quasibinomial)` ignored how many individuals each proportion was based on (`initial` ranges from 3 to 12 per replicate), so a 3-animal dish counted as much as a 12-animal dish; and (2) fitting each day in total isolation, with no shared information across days, gave wildly unstable estimates on days with little mortality spread (e.g. an LC50 of 4.2x10^16 g Cl for one group) and discarded the standard errors before plotting, so there was no way to see which day-specific estimates were trustworthy.

Instead, we fit one quasibinomial model per species x salt combination, using the actual survival counts (`cbind(n_surviving, n_dead)`, which supplies the sample size directly rather than via `weights`) and an `est_chloride * day` interaction. This pools information across days within a group and lets us formally test whether the dose-response relationship (and hence LC50) changes over time, via an F-test comparing the model with and without the interaction (appropriate here since `quasibinomial` doesn't have a well-defined likelihood for a chi-square LRT).

```{r lc50-models}
lc50_models = daily_prop_data %>% 
  filter(day != 0) %>% 
  mutate(n_dead = initial - n_surviving) %>% 
  group_by(species, salt) %>% 
  nest() %>% 
  mutate(
    model_full = map(data, ~ glm(cbind(n_surviving, n_dead) ~ est_chloride * day,
                                  data = .x, family = quasibinomial)),
    model_red  = map(data, ~ glm(cbind(n_surviving, n_dead) ~ est_chloride + day,
                                  data = .x, family = quasibinomial)),
    interaction_test = map2(model_red, model_full, ~ anova(.x, .y, test = "F"))
  )
```

```{r lc50-interaction-test}
interaction_summary = lc50_models %>% 
  mutate(
    f_stat = map_dbl(interaction_test, ~ .x$F[2]),
    p_value = map_dbl(interaction_test, ~ .x$`Pr(>F)`[2])
  ) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = "holm")) %>%  # 8 tests, one per species x salt
  dplyr::select(species, salt, f_stat, p_value, p_adj)

knitr::kable(interaction_summary, digits = 3,
             caption = "F-test for the est_chloride:day interaction (does the dose-response relationship change over time?) within each species x salt model. p_adj applies a Holm correction across the 8 tests.")
```

Only `L. sicilis` x RoadSalt shows a significant chloride:day interaction after correcting for multiple comparisons; the others are suggestive at best (uncorrected p ~ 0.09 for `L. sicilis`/NaCl and `Skistodiaptomus`/NaCl) or show no evidence of a time trend.

To visualize this, we convert each group's fitted intercept/slope-by-day into an LC50(day) trajectory with a delta-method confidence interval (the same approach `dose.p()` uses for a single model, extended here to a day-varying intercept and slope), evaluated only across the days actually observed within each species x salt group.

```{r lc50-trajectory}
lc50_trajectory = function(model, days) {
  cf = coef(model)
  vc = vcov(model)
  b0 = cf[["(Intercept)"]]; b1 = cf[["est_chloride"]]
  b2 = cf[["day"]];         b3 = cf[["est_chloride:day"]]

  map_dfr(days, function(d) {
    N = -(b0 + b2 * d)
    D = b1 + b3 * d
    lc50 = N / D
    grad = c(
      "(Intercept)"      = -1 / D,
      "est_chloride"     = -N / D^2,
      "day"              = -d / D,
      "est_chloride:day" = -N * d / D^2
    )
    grad = grad[rownames(vc)]
    se = sqrt(as.numeric(t(grad) %*% vc %*% grad))
    tibble(day = d, lc50 = lc50, se = se)
  })
}

day_range = daily_prop_data %>% 
  filter(day != 0) %>% 
  group_by(species, salt) %>% 
  summarise(min_day = min(day), max_day = max(day), .groups = "drop")

lc50_traj = lc50_models %>% 
  dplyr::select(species, salt, model_full) %>% 
  left_join(day_range, by = c("species", "salt")) %>% 
  mutate(
    traj = pmap(list(model_full, min_day, max_day), function(m, lo, hi) {
      lc50_trajectory(m, seq(lo, hi, length.out = 30))
    })
  ) %>% 
  dplyr::select(species, salt, traj) %>% 
  unnest(traj) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(
    lc50_g = lc50 / 1000,
    lwr_g = pmax((lc50 - 1.96 * se) / 1000, 0),
    upr_g = (lc50 + 1.96 * se) / 1000
  )
```

```{r lc50-trajectory-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}
ggplot(lc50_traj, aes(x = day, y = lc50_g, colour = salt, fill = salt)) + 
  facet_wrap(species ~ salt, scales = "free") + 
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr_g, ymax = upr_g), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) + 
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = salt_cols) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = salt_cols) + 
  labs(x = "Day", y = "LC50 (g Chloride / L)") + 
  theme_matt_facets() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The ribbon width makes the earlier instability visible rather than hiding it: for example, the `L. sicilis`/NaCl and `Skistodiaptomus`/MgCl2 trajectories carry very wide intervals at the days where the interaction test above was non-significant, meaning those day-to-day changes in LC50 shouldn't be over-interpreted. The `RoadSalt` trajectories (and `L. sicilis`/MgCl2) are comparatively well-identified across the full day range.
